text: Welcome to Four Eyes Report. Two stories this week: one about a missile, and one about an alphabet.
An alphabet? In the same sentence as a missile? Bold.
It's that kind of week. Let's start with the fast one. Ms. Nonfic.
Good evening. On October eighth, South Korea test-launched its first hypersonic glide vehicle, or H G V, developed by the Agency for Defense Development.
Hypersonic glide vehicle. That's three words I need explained.
Hypersonic means at least five times the speed of sound. Mach five. About six thousand one hundred kilometers an hour.
Wait. Don't ballistic missiles already go that fast?
Many do. The difference is the path. A ballistic missile flies a high arc, up and down, like a thrown ball. You can calculate where it lands.
And the glider?
A rocket booster carries it high up. Then it separates and glides down through the atmosphere at lower altitude, and it can change direction.
A thrown ball versus a paper airplane. A very fast, very serious paper airplane.
I would not use the term paper airplane. But the physics is not wrong.
Why is that so hard to stop?
Three reasons. One: it flies low, and the curve of the Earth is in the way of ground radar, so it can be spotted later.
Two: missile defenses predict where a target will be, then aim there. If the target keeps changing course, the prediction keeps missing.
Three: less time. By the time it is seen, the window to respond can be a matter of minutes.
So it's impossible to stop?
Nobody serious says impossible. They say difficult. I prefer accurate to dramatic.
And what's hard about building one?
Heat. At these speeds, friction with the air heats the surface far past a thousand degrees. It needs special heat-resistant materials.
And a communication problem. The heat can turn the air around the vehicle into plasma, which can block radio signals.
So it's flying fast and can't call home.
So what did Korea's test check? Officials listed flight path and speed, heat protection, guidance and control, and low-altitude maneuvering.
The presidential office says the vehicle separated from its booster, followed its planned path, adjusted course horizontally and vertically at low altitude, and hit its target.
Speed and range were not disclosed. The site was not officially disclosed either. Yonhap reported a barge at a test center in Taean. That part is reported, not confirmed.
"Reported, not confirmed." That's Ms. Nonfic's love language.
President Lee Jae Myung attended with the defense minister. He said the government will fully support the development and operational deployment of advanced weaponry.
He also said the team must not rest on today's success, and that national security should rest on Korea's own strength.
The same day, he inspected the Hyunmoo-5, a surface-to-surface missile nicknamed the monster missile. Officials used that name in a press statement for the first time.
The monster missile. The naming department had a good day.

The timing matters. On October third, North Korea test-fired what Seoul assessed as a hypersonic medium-range ballistic missile. Seoul put its range at seven hundred kilometers. North Korea claimed one thousand.
So it's a race.
I would not call it a race. I would call it a pattern.
Is Korea building anything else in this area?
Yes. HyCore. It is a different type: a hypersonic cruise missile. It keeps its engine running the whole way, using a scramjet. ADD and Hyundai Rotem have worked on it since twenty eighteen.
Scramjet. What's that?
An engine that burns fuel in air rushing past faster than sound. Think of keeping a candle lit in a hurricane.
In a twenty twenty-four test, HyCore passed Mach six at an altitude of twenty-three kilometers. The partners aim to begin mass production by twenty thirty-five.
Twenty thirty-five. So the future is nine years away.
I will update the facts as they change. I do not update opinions. I do not have any.
Last story, a softer one. Last Friday, October ninth, was Hangul Day. Our historian, Dr. H.
Last time, I told you who made Hangul. This time, the holiday itself has a birthday. It turned one hundred.
The holiday is a hundred? Who threw the first party?
In nineteen twenty-six, the Korean Language Society held the first celebration, for the four hundred eightieth anniversary of the fourteen forty-six text.
What was it called?
"Gagya Day." It comes from the opening syllables of the Korean alphabet chart: ga, gya, geo, gyeo.
So it was literally Alphabet Day. Like "A-B-C Day."
Two years later, in nineteen twenty-eight, it was renamed Hangul Day. And the date moved several times before it settled on October ninth.
It lost its day off in the early nineties. In the mid-two-thousands it became an official national day again, but still without a day off. The day off came back in twenty thirteen.
A holiday that got laid off and rehired.
Why is it in the news? Because of foreign learners. This week, the King Sejong Institute Foundation invited a record three hundred fifty-seven Korean learners to Korea.
A hundred eighty-one of them came to a speaking and writing contest, from seventy-one countries.
Seventy-one countries. That's more than I've visited, even in my head.
The speaking contest had about two hundred eighty-four applicants for every finalist spot.
That's harder than getting concert tickets.
The grand prize in speaking went to Marjan Haghi of Iran. In writing, it went to Nguyen Bao Chau of Vietnam.
The writing finalists wrote their essays wearing Joseon-era scholar robes.
Finally, a dress code for homework.

Why do they learn Korean? A King Sejong Institute survey found "Korean content, such as K-pop, dramas, and movies" was the top reason, at fifty-three point four percent. It was the first time that answer ranked number one.
So the idol songs were homework in disguise.
One learner from Cairo, Amira Kamal Mohamed, started with the K-pop group EXO. She has studied Korean for ten years. She said it feels like she's inside a K-drama.
A learner from Canada, who started with K-pop in twenty nineteen, said that being able to read it makes her feel her Korean has really improved.
Reading is the real level-up. The first time I read a menu, I felt like I'd won a trophy.
And it's not only fandom. A foundation survey in twenty twenty-five found fifty point nine percent of foreign learners were preparing to study in Korea. Thirty-seven percent cited career goals.
So it's not just a crush. It's a plan.
And that's the point of Hangul. King Sejong wanted ordinary people to read and write. Five hundred eighty years later, they're still learning it, sometimes from a song.
Let's wrap up. A hypersonic test, and an alphabet.
Core, what's your take?
My take: speed makes the headlines. But what people are still choosing to learn, five hundred eighty years later, is an alphabet.
And the missile?
I'll leave that one to Ms. Nonfic. She doesn't have opinions.
And the alphabet?
The alphabet wins. One hundred years of a holiday, and people are still learning it. Thanks for watching.
